citizen.blurb: A reusable playbook that teaches an AI how to do a particular job.
citizen.standfirst: What a Skill actually is, how it differs from the AI being "trained," and why the same request gets handled the same careful way every time you ask.
citizen.core:
Ask a new hire and a veteran to file an expense report. The veteran knows the company’s way: which form to use, which receipts count, and who must approve it.

A skill gives an AI assistant that same know-how right away.

A skill is a written set of steps for a specific job. It can include rules, examples, formats, and tools to use. When a task matches, the assistant loads the skill and follows it.

This is not new training. The model itself does not change. A person or team simply gives it extra instructions for the job, much like giving a new hire a clear guide before their first shift.

An assistant can have many skills and use the one that best fits the task.
citizen.everyday:
Say you ask an AI to “summarize this the way I like it.” Without a skill, you may need to repeat your preferences each time.

A skill can save those instructions so the assistant can use them again. You do not have to type the same rules in every chat.

You may never write a skill yourself, but you can still benefit from one. A shopping assistant might always check your size and budget. A travel planner might always choose an aisle seat. A writing tool might always follow your company’s style.

The main benefit is consistency. The same kind of task can be handled the same way each time.
citizen.businesses:
Every company has its own rules and ways of working. Skills let a business turn that know-how into steps an AI assistant can follow.

A bank might use a skill that lists the fields needed in a loan summary. An airline might use one that explains which refund rules apply to each fare type.

Skills can improve consistency and make reviews easier. A compliance team can open the skill file and see what the assistant was told to do. When a rule changes, the team can update the skill instead of changing the AI model.

But skills need upkeep. If no one updates them, they can keep giving old guidance.
citizen.appBuilders:
Skills let you add reliable workflows without changing the model.

A skill can hold the steps, format, examples, and tools for one task. When the task appears, the assistant loads that file and follows it.

This can also make problems easier to fix. If the assistant handles refunds the wrong way, you can inspect and update the refund skill. You can also show that file to explain why the assistant acted as it did.
citizen.modelBuilders:
From the model’s point of view, a skill is extra context given at the right time.

The hard part is choosing when to load each skill. That gets harder as the assistant gains more skills and must pick the best one for each task.
citizen.smalltalk: A skill is a cheat sheet an AI reads before a job, so it follows your steps instead of guessing.

technical.blurb: Instructions an agent loads into context only when a task matches, distinct from a schema-bound tool call and no change to the model itself.
technical.standfirst: Progressive disclosure, why a Skill has no input/output schema the way a tool call does, how selection depends entirely on its description, and the failure modes that show up when the wrong Skill gets picked.
technical.core:
A skill is a bundle of instructions, plain text plus optionally scripts,
templates, or reference data, that an agent loads into its context
conditionally, only when a task actually matches it. Practically, this
means each skill ships as its own file or directory: a short description
the agent's selection step checks against the current request, and a
full body of instructions loaded into context only once that match
happens, staying out of every unrelated conversation entirely.

The common mix-up here is treating a skill as a special case of a tool
call. Tool calls have a fixed schema, defined parameters and a defined
return type, invoked programmatically mid-generation, with the result
fed back into the model's context. A skill has no schema; it's
unstructured instructions the model reads and reasons over like any
other prompt text, even though a skill can itself instruct the model to
invoke tools along the way.
technical.appBuilders:
Skills solve a real context-budget problem: an agent with fifty possible
procedures can't have all fifty spelled out in full in every prompt
without drowning the useful signal in irrelevant instructions. Instead,
you attach a short description to each skill, one or two sentences an
agent uses at selection time, and only load the full instruction body
for the skill that actually matches the request at hand.

This has direct engineering consequences. Selection quality depends
heavily on how distinctly worded each skill's description is; two skills
with overlapping descriptions get mis-selected against each other more
often as you add more skills to the roster. It also changes how you debug
production issues: if an agent handled a task wrong, check first whether
the right skill got selected at all before assuming the instructions
inside it were bad, since those are two different bug classes with
different fixes. And because a skill is an ordinary file, a fix ships the moment
the file changes, with no retraining or redeployment of the model itself.
Some frameworks also let a skill reference a script file directly, so
instructions can hand off deterministic steps to actual code that runs
them.
technical.businesses:
Skills give a technical team a way to encode compliance-sensitive
procedures, required disclosures, approval sequences, and formatting
mandates, as auditable, versioned files a reviewer can open and diff
against a prior version before it reaches production. A reviewer can
read the exact instructions the agent followed for a given output,
which matters in regulated domains where a decision has to hold up to
explanation long after it was made, sometimes during a formal audit.

The operational cost is maintenance overhead at scale: an organization
running dozens of skills needs a real process for reviewing and testing
changes to them, the same discipline you'd apply to any other
production configuration, because a broken skill produces broken output
in every conversation that matches it until someone catches it. Skills
also introduce a selection failure mode distinct from prompt-injection
risk. A task can silently invoke the wrong skill's procedure, a
correctness bug that needs its own monitoring separate from security
review, since nothing about a wrong-skill selection looks anomalous to
a system watching for malicious input.
technical.modelBuilders:
From the model's perspective, a skill is ordinary context injected at
inference time: no architecture change, no fine-tuning step, nothing
persisted across sessions. The harder problem sits upstream of the model:
designing the selection mechanism that decides which skill's instructions
to load, since a model given the wrong skill will follow it faithfully and
still produce the wrong output. Some implementations lean on the model
itself to read short descriptions and pick a match; others use a separate
retrieval step entirely outside the model call.
technical.smalltalk:
A skill's a set of instructions an AI agent loads only when the task
actually calls for it, handing someone exactly the one manual they need
right then.
